question: I'm applying from India for a German student visa. Do I need an APS certificate?
answer: Generally yes: for a German student visa applied for in India, an APS certificate is always mandatory unless an exception applies [S2]. You do not need one if: you obtain a non-German degree in Germany; you plan PhD/postdoc studies; you received a scholarship from German or EU public funds; or your studies build on a non-Indian school certificate (e.g. International Baccalaureate) or a non-Indian degree [S2]. This checklist was last updated in September 2024, so confirm it is still current [S4]. Universities may also require APS for admission: TUM, for example, requires applicants with an Indian school or university degree to have their certificates checked by APS in New Delhi and attend an interview [S5]. Your visa category matters too: if you need an APS certificate, your appointment will be at VFS [S1]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with the German mission or VFS.

question: What kind of account do most international students use to prove they can pay for their studies in Germany?
answer:
Most international students use a blocked account, called a "Sperrkonto," as proof of funds, with the funds shown as a credit to the account [S1]. Key points:

- The required amount rose from €11,208 a year (since 1 January 2023) to €11,904 a year from January 2025 [S1]. The German consulate checklist for India also states €11,904 for your first year, with no more than €992 withdrawable per month [S4].
- A Sperrkonto limits monthly withdrawals, and you can only close it with approval from an embassy, consulate or the competent foreigners authority [S1].
- Alternatives include proof of your parents' income and assets, a guarantor in Germany, a recognised scholarship, or an annually renewable bank guarantee from a bank in Germany [S1].

The DAAD recommends getting advice from the German embassy or consulate [S1]. This is not legal advice; please confirm current requirements with them.

question: If I finish a degree in Germany but need time to find a job, how long can I stay on the post-study permit?
answer:
After you graduate in Germany, you can extend your residence permit by up to 18 months to look for a job that suits your qualifications [S2][S5]. In Hamburg's guidance this is a residence permit under § 20 Para. 1 No. 1 AufenthG for 18 months [S1].

Key conditions:
- You must prove you can cover your living costs and that you have health insurance [S2][S3].
- During these 18 months you may work in any job without restriction, including self-employment [S2][S3].
- If you find a suitable job, you can get a residence permit for employment [S2].
- Stays abroad longer than six months automatically end the permit unless the Foreigners Registration Department has agreed in writing beforehand [S3].
- This option is only available immediately after graduation [S1].

This is not legal advice. Please confirm the details with your local Foreigners Registration Department.

question: While I'm on the 18-month job-search permit after graduating in Germany, am I allowed to work?
answer:
Yes. During the up to 18-month job-search period after graduating, you are allowed to work, and you can do any job [S2]. The BAMF brochure says you are authorized for employment without restriction during this time (section 16 subs. 4 Residence Act) [S3]. The Hamburg guidance adds that this includes any internship or trainee post, and that you may also work self-employed or as a freelancer [S4].

Key conditions:
- You must prove that you can cover your living expenses for this period and that you have health insurance [S2][S4].
- If you complete an internship abroad, a stay outside Germany longer than six months automatically leads to the permit lapsing, unless the Foreigners Registration Department has agreed to a longer period in writing beforehand [S4].

This is not legal advice. Please confirm your situation with your local foreigners' authority.

question: In Germany, should I usually book a specialist directly, or start with a general doctor?
answer: Usually, you should start with a general practitioner (GP, Hausarzt). In most cases it is best to see a GP first, who will assess whether you need a specialist [S3]. GPs can treat most common illnesses and will refer you to a specialist if required [S1]. However, if you already know your illness needs a specialist, such as a dermatologist, you can contact that specialist directly [S1]. Whether you can book a specialist yourself depends on the medical field; for toothache or a dental check-up, you can book a dental practice directly [S2]. Be aware that specialist appointments can take some time to get [S2]. Check in advance that the practice accepts your health insurance [S1]. This is general guidance, not legal or medical advice; confirm details with your insurer or university.

question: Can a student residence permit in Munich cover a required preparatory language course before a full-time degree?
answer: Yes. In Munich, a residence permit for the purpose of studying also covers preparatory measures such as a preparatory language course [S1]. The condition is that you already have a guaranteed place on a full-time degree programme at the relevant educational institution [S1]. If your admission is only conditional, or you are doing other preparatory study, granting the permit is at the discretion of the Service Centre for Immigration and Naturalisation [S1]. In that case a separate study-preparation permit may apply instead. It requires a university entrance qualification or a conditional offer, and a preparatory language course is limited to a maximum of 18 months [S2]. Berlin's guidance also says a language course counts as preparation when admission is tied to attending it [S3]. Please confirm your case with the Munich authority; this is not legal advice.

question: What should I do at Sabancı after submitting my Turkish residence permit file, and who decides the outcome?
answer: After you hand your file to the IRO, it is forwarded to the Istanbul Provincial Immigration Administration, and you should regularly check the Immigration Office website (e-ikamet) for updates, because the result comes to you by email/SMS and on that website within 30-90 days [S1]. The IRO does not receive application results, so tracking is up to you [S1]. It can take up to 90 days for approval and card preparation, and the card is sent to the address on your address document; tracking the card is your personal responsibility [S1]. If you gave the Tuzla Campus as your address, the Communication Center will notify you when the card arrives [S1]. Once you have it, send a copy to irolegal@sabanciuniv.edu and studentinfo@sabanciuniv.edu [S1]. Leaving Türkiye before you get the card is not recommended, as it may lead to rejection [S5]. The Directorate General of Migration Management decides the outcome, not the university [S1][S5]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with the authority.

question: How soon after getting a residence permit card should I register my address at Sabancı?
answer:
You must register your address within 20 days of receiving your residence permit card [S1]. If your address later changes, you must register the new address as well [S1]. Erasmus and Exchange students can skip this step if they will not extend their permits in Türkiye [S1].

Key conditions and steps:
- Book an appointment through the Immigration Office Appointment System, which requires e-devlet access, and attend in person on the appointment day [S1].
- You must be over 18, your card must be active, and you must be in İstanbul [S2].
- If you live in the university dormitories or in Tuzla, Pendik, Kartal, Maltepe, Şile, Adalar or Kadıköy, register at the Pendik District Immigration Office [S2].
- Afterwards, you can get a residence certificate (Yerleşim Yeri Belgesi) from e-Devlet, which is needed for permit extensions [S2].

This is not legal advice; please confirm with the Immigration Office or the IRO.

question: If I want to use Turkish GSS as an international student, how long after university registration do I have to apply?
answer: You must apply for General Health Insurance (GSS) within three months following your university registration [S1][S2]. Sabancı University specifies this means your first registration to the university, and that you apply after receiving your foreign national ID number, at the Social Security City Directorate or the Social Security Center (SGM) of the district where you live [S4]. GSS is available to international students who have a residence permit card and are registered at a Turkish university [S4]. If you miss the 3-month period, you cannot benefit from GSS afterward [S3][S4]. However, if you change your program or program level (e.g. undergraduate to master's), you have the right to apply again [S3]. These processes are managed by state bodies and are open to change, so please confirm with the Social Security Institution before relying on this; this is not legal advice [S3].

question: Are private health insurance policies in Türkiye accepted at every hospital?
answer: No. Private health insurance policies in Türkiye have limited coverage and are only valid in hospitals where the insurance company has a contract [S1][S3]. The insurer must have an agreement with the relevant hospital, so you may not be able to use your policy everywhere [S2]. Sabancı University also notes they can be used in private hospitals only, and that limits drop with each process, so expensive hospitals can use up your coverage quickly [S2]. Within the limits in your policy, you get free services at contracted hospitals, so get an English copy and read it carefully [S4]. By contrast, General Health Insurance (GSS) lets you be treated free of charge in all state hospitals [S1]. This is general information, not legal advice; check your policy and confirm with your insurer or university.

question: What kinds of housing can an international student look at in Türkiye?
answer: In Türkiye you can choose between university dormitories on campus, state dormitories run by KYK (Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution) in various parts of the city, private dormitories, or a rented apartment in the city [S2]. Private dormitories are found around most university campuses and usually offer better facilities than state dormitories, such as newer furniture, but they cost more [S1]. If you rent, many students share a house with a few friends in neighborhoods close to universities [S1]. Prices vary by city, location and the features of the house [S1]. Homes are usually apartments with a large living room and 2 to 4 bedrooms [S1]. The sources do not give specific prices or application steps for dormitories, so check details with your university or the dormitory directly.

question: Does a Turkish student residence permit itself give me permission to take a paid job?
answer:
No. Your student residence permit does not automatically give you the right to work in Türkiye; you need an official work permit [S1]. You cannot apply for it yourself: you first find a job, and the employer applies for your work permit [S1]. Applications are made to the Ministry of Labour and Social Security [S3].

Key conditions:
- Associate/undergraduate students: work rights start only after the first year of study [S3][S5], only for part-time jobs [S1], with a maximum of 24 hours per week [S5].
- Graduate students: you can get a work permit from your first year, for full-time or part-time jobs [S1].
- Both levels: METU says permits are only for jobs outside the university/campus [S1].

If you work without a work permit, the Migration Office could cancel your residence permit [S4]. This is not legal advice; confirm with the Ministry or the Migration Office before you start working.

question: Does the German student visa checklist for Indian applicants require a passport with just one blank page?
answer: No. The German Missions in India checklist (last updated September 2024) asks for a valid passport issued within the last 10 years with at least 2 empty pages, so one blank page is not enough [S1][S2]. You should also bring a signed application form (2 copies) and an A4 copy of your passport's data page (2 copies) [S1]. Other German missions set the same two-page minimum. The UK mission asks for 2 consecutive blank pages and a passport valid for at least six months [S3]. The Canada mission asks for 2 subsequent blank pages [S4]. This is not legal advice; please confirm the current requirements with the German Mission in India before your appointment.

question: I'm 29 and studying in Germany. Roughly how much is statutory student health insurance per month?
answer: The sources give somewhat different figures for statutory (public) student health insurance if you are under 30: about €120–130 per month [S1], around €110 per month [S2], and about €140 per month [S5]. One visa checklist also budgets €137 per month for insurance costs [S3]. All sources were retrieved on the same date (2026-11-18), so none is clearly more recent; S1 and S2 are DAAD publications. Since you're 29, the student rate applies to you for now, but be aware that once you turn 30 you'll pay the standard contribution [S1], which one source puts at €250 or more per month [S5]. At that point, private insurance may be cheaper [S1]. Please confirm the current rate with a statutory insurer; this is not legal advice.

question: If I want to stay and look for work after graduating, how do the options in Germany and Türkiye compare?
answer: Germany: the sources describe a specific job-search residence permit, but they do not describe an equivalent for Türkiye. In Germany, you can apply for a residence permit under § 20 Para. 1 No. 1 AufenthG for 18 months to look for a job, but only immediately after graduation [S4]. If you first take a job abroad, you lose that option and would instead need a 12-month 'Chance card' visa from a German mission abroad, which does not allow unrestricted work [S4]. With a German degree, you can usually join the labour market directly [S3]. Türkiye: the sources only mention practical help, such as campus career fairs and university career-centre services [S1]. They also say a student residence permit does not include permission to work [S5]. They do not say whether Türkiye offers a post-graduation job-search permit or how to stay after your studies, so that part is not covered. This is not legal advice; please confirm with the immigration authorities.

question: I have a student residence permit from France and want to study one semester in Germany. Do I need a German residence permit?
answer: The sources only partly answer this, and the answer depends on your programme and nationality. If you are a non-EU (third-country) student coming from a KIT partner university in Europe on an exchange programme, KIT says you must apply for a confirmation of Mobility within the EU under the REST Directive (EU Directive 2016/801) [S1]. The sources do not say whether this confirmation removes the need for a German residence permit, or how mobility works at other German universities. The general rule given is that non-EU citizens studying in Germany for more than 90 days must apply for a residence permit at the local foreigners' registration office within the first three months [S3]. EU/EEA/Swiss citizens need no residence permit [S1]. Please check with your host university's International Office and the local foreigners' office. This is not legal advice, and the rules can change.

question: Do student assistant jobs at my university count toward my work-day limit in Germany?
answer:
Generally, no: according to the sources, jobs as an academic or research assistant at your university do not count toward your limit, and there is no limit on how many days you may work [S2][S4]. The standard limit for other jobs is 140 full days per calendar year [S5][S1]. Conditions:
- The sources differ on what you must do. The DAAD sources say you only have to inform the foreigners' office [S2][S4]. TUM says you need authorization from the Foreigners' Office in your residence permit [S5]. All are dated the same, so check this with your office.
- If you are unsure whether your job is in this category, ask student services or your Foreigners Registration Department office [S2][S3].
- Breaking the work rules can lead to deportation [S2].

This is not legal advice. Confirm your situation with your local foreigners' office.

question: Does my student residence permit let me work in Germany, and is it the same in Türkiye?
answer:
For Germany, the sources don't say whether a student residence permit lets you work. They only explain that non-EU students must apply for a residence permit for the purpose of studying at the foreigners' office [S4]. Please check this with the local foreigners' office.

In Türkiye, your residence permit does not automatically give you the right to work; you need an official work permit [S2][S3]. You cannot apply for it yourself. You first find a job, and then the employer applies for your work permit [S2].
- Undergraduates: only after the first year, only part-time, and only for jobs off campus [S2].
- Graduate students: from the first year, full-time or part-time, but only off campus [S2].

If you work without a work permit, the Migration Office could cancel your residence permit [S1].

This is not legal advice; rules can change, so confirm with the responsible authority.
